## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** Native mobile accessibility as a design decision, plus the current legal enforcement landscape for digital accessibility. Narrow scope — two related halves. HALF ONE, native platform accessibility that a DESIGNER must decide, not a developer: (1) Apple Dynamic Type — the text style ramp, what sizes the accessibility sizes reach, what a designer must commit to for a layout to survive the largest accessibility text sizes, and Apple's stated guidance on layouts that must reflow or switch to vertical at large sizes; (2) VoiceOver on iOS — accessibility traits, labels vs hints vs values, the rotor and heading structure, what a designer decides about reading order and grouping; (3) Android TalkBack and the Android accessibility model — content descriptions, touch exploration, the recommended 48dp target and its relationship to WCAG, and Android's font scaling including non-linear font scaling introduced in Android 14; (4) what accessibility requirements differ between native and web such that a web-derived checklist misses them entirely. HALF TWO, legal drivers and their CURRENT enforcement state as of 2026: (5) the European Accessibility Act (Directive EU 2019/882) — what became applicable in June 2025, exactly which products and services are in scope, the microenterprise exemption and its thresholds, and what standard conformance is measured against (EN 301 549 and its relationship to WCAG); (6) the US DOJ ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR part 35 subpart H) — the technical standard it names, and its compliance deadlines by public entity size; (7) Section 508 and what standard it currently references; (8) whether any binding instrument yet names WCAG 2.2 rather than 2.1 or 2.0. Prioritize primary sources only: developer.apple.com Human Interface Guidelines accessibility pages, developer.android.com accessibility docs, EUR-Lex official directive text, ada.gov and the Federal Register, and the ETSI EN 301 549 standard text. Reject law-firm marketing blogs and accessibility-vendor content marketing where a primary source exists.

19 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] Apple's iOS/iPadOS Dynamic Type ramp has 7 standard sizes (xSmall through xxxLarge, default = Large) plus 5 larger accessibility sizes AX1-AX5, and the Body text style scales from 17pt at the default to 53pt at AX5 - roughly 3.1x. Large Title runs 34pt to 60pt over the same range.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography (primary)
Quote: "Large (default) … Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold … iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes … AX5 … Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold"
Verifier evidence (high): Tried to refute; every number checks out against Apple's own data. Fetched the HIG typography page's backing DocC JSON (https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.json — the rendered HTML page is JS-only, so WebFetch returns nothing useful) and parsed the spec tables verbatim.

(1) "7 standard sizes, default = Large": section "iOS, iPadOS Dynamic Type sizes" contains exactly 7 subsection tables — xSmall, Small, Medium, "Large (default)", xLarge, xxLarge, xxxLarge. Confirmed, including that Large is the one Apple labels default.

(2) "5 accessibility sizes AX1-AX5": a separate section titled "iOS, iPadOS larger accessibility type sizes" contains exactly 5 tables — AX1, AX2, AX3, AX4, AX5. Confirmed.

(3) "Body 17pt → 53pt, roughly 3.1x": Large (default) row = "Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold". AX5 row = "Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold". 53/17 = 3.118, so "roughly 3.1x" is accurate, not rounded favorably. The full Body ramp is 17 / 28 / 33 / 40 / 47 / 53 (Large, AX1-AX5).

(4) "Large Title 34pt → 60pt": Large (default) = "Large Title | Regular | 34 | 41 | Bold"; AX5 = "Large Title | Regular | 60 | 70 | Bold". Confirmed. (My prior expectation was 58 at AX5 — the source says 60, so the claim is right and my recollection was wrong.) Full Large Title ramp: 34 / 44 / 48 / 52 / 56 / 60.

Currency: the page's own change log lists "December 16, 2025 — Added emphasized weights to the Dynamic Type style specifications for each platform" as the most recent revision, so this is the live spec as of August 2026, not a stale table. The supporting quote in the claim ("Body | Regular | 17 | 22 | Semibold" and AX5 "Body | Regular | 53 | 62 | Semibold") reproduces the emphasized-weight column added in that Dec 2025 revision, which corroborates it was read from the current page rather than an older cached copy.

Source quality: primary (Apple, first-party normative spec). No vendor blog or law-firm content involved. WebSearch for contradicting values surfaced only secondary write-ups (Medium/UX Collective/dept engineering), none of which dispute these figures; one independently states 12 total sizes and ~310% body scaling at AX5, consistent with the claim.

Non-refuting caveat worth carrying forward into the design guidance rather than treated as an error: the scaling is not uniform across styles — Body goes 3.1x while Large Title goes only 1.76x (34→60), and at AX5 Body (53) is larger than the default Large Title (34) and nearly equal to Headline (53) and Title 3 (55). That is the actual designer-facing consequence and it strengthens rather than undercuts the claim.

### [1] Apple explicitly instructs designers to switch to a stacked (vertical) layout at large font sizes, naming inline glyphs, timestamps and container boundaries as the specific elements that crowd text and cause truncation or overlap in horizontally constrained contexts.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography (primary)
Quote: "Consider adjusting your layout at large font sizes. When font size increases in a horizontally constrained context, inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries can crowd text and cause truncation or overlapping. To improve readability, consider using a stacked layout where text appears above secondary items."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED at the primary source. WebFetch on the rendered HIG page returns only a JS shell, so I pulled Apple's own DocC data endpoint: `curl https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography.json` (HTTP 200, 279KB). Grepping it yields exactly one occurrence each of "stacked", "horizontally constrained", "timestamp", "container bound", "crowd", and "adjusting your layout", in a single paragraph node:

strong: "Consider adjusting your layout at large font sizes." + text: " When font size increases in a horizontally constrained context, inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries can crowd text and cause truncation or overlapping. To improve readability, consider using a stacked layout where text appears above secondary items. Multicolumn text can also be less readable at large sizes due to horizontal space constraints. Reduce the number of columns when the font size increases to avoid truncation and enhance readability."

So the supporting quote is word-for-word accurate, not paraphrased or stitched. Context: the bullet sits in the Dynamic Type best-practices run of the Typography page, immediately after "Make sure your app's layout adapts to all font sizes," "Increase the size of meaningful interface icons as font size increases," and "Keep text truncation to a minimum as font size increases."

CURRENCY: page metadata customMetadata.alert-date = "2025-12-16" ("Added emphasized weights to the Dynamic Type style specifications for each platform"), supported-platforms ios,ipados,macos,tvos,visionos,watchos — i.e. this is the live, recently-maintained page as of 2026-08-01, not an archived HIG. Independent search corroboration returned the same sentence, plus an older/looser HIG wording ("At large font sizes, an inline layout might cause text to truncate...consider using a stacked layout"), showing this guidance has persisted across HIG revisions rather than being a one-off. No source disputes or qualifies it.

ELEMENT-BY-ELEMENT: "stacked (vertical)" is a fair gloss of "text appears above secondary items"; "inline glyphs, timestamps and container boundaries" maps exactly onto "inline items (like glyphs and timestamps) and container boundaries"; "crowd text and cause truncation or overlap in horizontally constrained contexts" is verbatim.

ONE QUALIFICATION (not fatal, but downstream copy should not harden it): Apple's modality is advisory — "Consider adjusting…", "consider using a stacked layout" — not a mandate. The claim's "explicitly instructs designers to switch" overstates the verb slightly. The guidance is explicit and unambiguous, and the whole HIG is advisory by construction, so the substance holds; but "Apple recommends considering a stacked layout" is the defensible phrasing, and "requires/instructs" should not be used if the claim is later cited as a hard rule.

### [2] Apple's HIG accessibility page sets an explicit text-enlargement target designers must design for: at least 200 percent enlargement (140 percent on watchOS), achievable either through custom UI or by adopting Dynamic Type.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (primary)
Quote: "**Support larger text sizes.** Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type."
Verifier evidence (high): VERIFIED VERBATIM against the primary source, not a paraphrase. WebFetch failed (Apple HIG is JS-rendered), so I pulled the page's backing JSON directly: `curl https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.json` → HTTP 200, 88,675 bytes, identifier `doc://com.apple.HIG/design/Human-Interface-Guidelines/accessibility`. Grepping the JSON returns exactly one hit for "200", one for "custom UI", one for "larger text", inside a single bolded bullet in the "Vision" section (anchor `#Vision`, immediately after "The people who use your interface may be blind, color blind, or have low vision or light sensitivity"):

"**Support larger text sizes.** Make sure people can adjust the size of your text or icons to make them more legible, visible, and comfortable to read. Ideally, give people the option to enlarge text by at least 200 percent (or 140 percent in watchOS apps). Your interface can support font size enlargement either through custom UI, or by adopting Dynamic Type."

Every load-bearing element of the claim matches character-for-character: the 200 percent floor, the 140 percent watchOS carve-out, and the explicit either/or of custom UI vs. Dynamic Type. The supporting quote as given in the claim is not fabricated or reconstructed.

CURRENCY: the page's own Change log table (extracted from the same JSON) is topped by "June 9, 2025 — Added guidance and links for Assistive Access, Switch Control, and Accessibility Nutrition Labels," preceded by "March 7, 2025 — Expanded and refined all guidance. Moved Dynamic Type guidance to the Typography page, and moved VoiceOver guidance to a new VoiceOver page." So this bullet survived the most recent full rewrite of the page and is live as fetched today (2026-08-01). Not outdated.

CORROBORATION (independent Apple primary source, not vendor content): developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria — the Accessibility Nutrition Labels "Larger Text" criteria — independently states apps must let "users enlarge text to at least 200% or the maximum font size for the system," confirms watchOS's largest Dynamic Type size exceeds 140% of default and that support may be shown "by implementing Dynamic Type or by supporting an equivalent or larger size for body text," and explicitly permits non-Dynamic-Type custom implementations (citing Apple Books, which reflows two columns to one at large sizes). Two independent Apple primary sources agree on both numbers and on the two-path implementation.

ONE QUALIFIER, not fatal: Apple's word is "Ideally," which frames the 200%/140% figure as a strong recommendation, not a hard mandate. The claim's "designers must design for" is marginally stronger than the HIG's own hedge. It is not an overreach in substance, however — the claim's operative assertion is that the HIG "sets an explicit text-enlargement target," which it demonstrably does, and the App Store Connect criteria page converts the same numbers into a pass/fail evaluation threshold for any app declaring Larger Text support, which supplies the "must" the HIG softens. A downstream writer should attribute the number as Apple's stated target while preserving "ideally."

No contradicting source found. Source is the exact primary source the research brief prioritizes (developer.apple.com HIG accessibility page); no law-firm or vendor content involved.

### [3] Apple's recommended minimum control size for iOS/iPadOS is 44x44 pt default with a 28x28 pt hard minimum — a per-platform table (macOS 28x28/20x20, tvOS 66x66/56x56, visionOS 60x60/28x28, watchOS 44x44/28x28) that differs from Android's 48dp recommendation and from any single web-derived target rule.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility (primary)
Quote: "| Platform | Default control size | Minimum control size |
| iOS, iPadOS | 44x44 pt | 28x28 pt |
| macOS | 28x28 pt | 20x20 pt |
| tvOS | 66x66 pt | 56x56 pt |
| visionOS | 60x60 pt | 28x28 pt |
| watchOS | 44x44 pt | 28x28 pt |"
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM CONFIRMED on the primary source, live today (2026-08-01). WebFetch returns nothing (JS-rendered), so I pulled Apple's own DocC JSON backing the page: `curl https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility.json` → HTTP 200, 88,675 bytes. Under the "Mobility" H2, the prose reads: "**Offer sufficiently sized controls.** Controls that are too small are hard for many people to interact with and select. Strive to meet the recommended minimum control size for each platform to ensure controls and menus are comfortable for all when tapping and clicking." Immediately following is a `"type": "table", "header": "row"` whose cells decode to exactly: Platform / Default control size / Minimum control size — iOS, iPadOS 44x44 pt / 28x28 pt; macOS 28x28 pt / 20x20 pt; tvOS 66x66 pt / 56x56 pt; visionOS 60x60 pt / 28x28 pt; watchOS 44x44 pt / 28x28 pt. Every number in the claim matches character-for-character. Adjacent (also usable): "add about 12 points of padding around elements that include a bezel. For elements without a bezel, about 24 points of padding works well around the element's visible edges."

Comparative tail also verified primary: developer.android.com/guide/topics/ui/accessibility/apps — "we recommend that each interactive UI element have a focusable area, or touch target size, of at least 48dpx48dp. Larger is even better." So the Apple-vs-Android divergence the claim asserts is real.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS the downstream write-up MUST carry, or it will mislead designers:
(1) "hard minimum" is the claimant's gloss, not Apple's. Apple's verb is "Strive to meet" — aspirational floor, not an enforced one. Drop "hard".
(2) The table measures *control size*; it does NOT replace the 44x44 pt *hit region* rule, and Apple still publishes that rule elsewhere. developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons (fetched same way, HTTP 200) says verbatim: "As a general rule, a button needs a hit region of at least 44x44 pt — in visionOS, 60x60 pt — to ensure that people can select it easily, whether they use a fingertip, a pointer, their eyes, or a remote." Note the visionOS conflict in particular: accessibility table says minimum 28x28 pt, Buttons page says 60x60 pt hit region. Control frame and tappable area are different measures (a 28pt glyph inside a 44pt hit region satisfies both). Android's 48dp is explicitly the *focusable/touch-target* area, so the correct like-for-like comparison is Apple 44x44 pt hit region vs Android 48dp touch target — not 28x28 vs 48dp. Claim survives; the 28x28 number must be labeled "minimum control size, not minimum tappable area."

Not marketing, not vendor content, not outdated: fetched from Apple's own docs endpoint today. The 28x28/per-platform table is recent HIG guidance (post-visionOS-era revision) — most third-party summaries still repeat only the legacy "44x44 minimum", which is why the table is worth citing, with caveat (2) attached.

### [4] Apple states VoiceOver reads elements in the reading order of the user's active language and locale (top-to-bottom, left-to-right in US English), which means default reading order is derived from layout — so a designer must explicitly group related elements or VoiceOver will read all images before all captions rather than pairing each image with its caption.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover (primary)
Quote: "VoiceOver reads elements in the same order people read content in the their active language and locale. For example, in US English, this is top-to-bottom, left-to-right. In the ungrouped example below, VoiceOver describes each image before moving on to the captions. In the grouped example, VoiceOver describes each image with its respective caption."
Verifier evidence (high): VERBATIM MATCH CONFIRMED against the live primary source. I bypassed the JS-rendered HIG page by fetching Apple's own backing content API: https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover.json (HTTP 200, 36,827 bytes, fetched 2026-08-01). The page body contains, character-for-character:

"VoiceOver reads elements in the same order people read content in the their active language and locale. For example, in US English, this is top-to-bottom, left-to-right. In the ungrouped example below, VoiceOver describes each image before moving on to the captions. In the grouped example, VoiceOver describes each image with its respective caption."

Note the doubled article "in the their" — the typo is Apple's own, present in the live JSON, which corroborates that the supporting quote was transcribed from the source rather than paraphrased or fabricated.

CONTEXT SUPPORTS THE NORMATIVE HALF. The paragraph sits directly under Apple's bolded guideline heading "Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked." followed by: "Proximity, alignment, and other visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements. Examine your app for places where relationships among elements are visual only. Then, describe these relationships to VoiceOver." So the claim's "a designer must explicitly group related elements" is Apple's own imperative, not the claim's invention. The accompanying figures are keyed voiceover-incorrect-grouping.png (abstract: "Ungrouped related elements make it hard for VoiceOver to accurately describe the UI.", marked with crossout.png) and voiceover-correct-grouping.png (abstract: "Grouped related elements help VoiceOver accurately describe the UI.", marked with checkmark.png) — the mango/artichoke image-plus-caption example. Apple links to shouldGroupAccessibilityChildren for developer guidance.

CURRENCY. Page metadata: supported-platforms ios,ipados,macos,tvos,visionos,watchos; alert-text "New page."; alert-date 2025-03-07. It is a live, recently-added HIG page, retrieved today — not archived or superseded.

REFUTATION ATTEMPTS THAT FAILED. (1) I probed the strongest available counter-line, that iOS VoiceOver order is derived from the accessibility/view hierarchy rather than geometry (accessibilityElements in UIKit, .accessibility(sortPriority:) in SwiftUI, per developer.apple.com/documentation/uikit/supporting-voiceover-in-your-app and /documentation/swiftui/view/accessibility(sortpriority:)). This does NOT contradict the claim: those are override mechanisms a developer applies, and their existence presupposes a default the developer is overriding. Apple's design-level statement of that default is spatial ("top-to-bottom, left-to-right"), which is exactly what the claim renders as "derived from layout." The claim is also careful to attribute — "Apple states" — so it reports Apple's design guidance rather than asserting an independent engineering fact about the traversal algorithm. (2) No credible source disputes the operative conclusion; grouping related elements is uncontested accessibility guidance. (3) Source is Apple's own HIG, i.e. the definitive primary source for a claim about what Apple states — source quality exceeds the claim's strength.

MINOR CAVEATS, NOT REFUTATIONS. (a) The claim's word "designer" is the researcher's framing, though it is well-founded: the page lives under developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines and the guideline is phrased as a specification decision ("Specify how elements are grouped..."), with implementation deferred to a linked developer API. (b) Apple's own illustration alt text is internally loose — the "incorrect" figure's alt reads "The images and captions are all contained within a single VoiceOver frame," which describes over-grouping rather than the ungrouped reading order the body text describes. That is an inconsistency inside Apple's page, not in the claim, which tracks the body prose accurately. (c) "the user's active language and locale" slightly sharpens Apple's ambiguous "the their active language and locale" (app vs. user locale), which is immaterial to the substance.

Claim is accurately quoted, correctly interpreted, currently live, and sourced to the definitive primary authority.

### [5] Apple assigns the grouping/ordering/linking of interface elements as an explicit design responsibility, instructing designers to audit the UI for relationships that are conveyed by visual cues only (proximity, alignment) and then describe those relationships to VoiceOver.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover (primary)
Quote: "Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked. Proximity, alignment, and other visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements. Examine your app for places where relationships among elements are visual only. Then, describe these relationships to VoiceOver."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched the live JSON data backing https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover directly (the HTML is a JS SPA shell, so I pulled the underlying tutorials/data JSON that renders it) and found the supporting quote verbatim, word-for-word: "Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked. Proximity, alignment, and other visible contextual cues help sighted people perceive the relationships between elements. Examine your app for places where relationships among elements are visual only. Then, describe these relationships to VoiceOver." This sits under the page's "Navigation" H2 heading as one of several bolded best-practice bullets (alongside "Use titles and headings to help people navigate...", "Inform VoiceOver when visible content or layout changes occur.", etc.). Critically, the page's own structure supports the claim's design-vs-developer framing: immediately after this bullet's illustrative example (grouped vs. ungrouped screenshots), the page adds a separate line — "For developer guidance, see [shouldGroupAccessibilityChildren API reference]" — a pattern repeated after every bullet on the page. This confirms Apple treats the bullet text itself (examine/describe relationships) as the design-level instruction and cordons off the implementation mechanism as a distinct "developer guidance" pointer, which is exactly what the claim asserts (design responsibility = audit + describe; separate from the how-to-implement API). The claim's wording is a close, non-overreaching paraphrase of the primary text, not a stretch or misread. No contradicting or qualifying source found (WebSearch for related phrasing returned only paraphrases of the same passage, none disputing it). Source is the strongest possible primary source for this claim and the content is current (live fetch, no deprecation/version markers).

### [6] Apple's Dynamic Type ramp offers 7 text sizes by default, plus 5 additional "larger accessibility sizes" when the user enables them, for 12 total sizes an app layout must survive.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10074/ (primary)
Quote: "By default, there are 7 available text sizes to chose from. If larger accessibility sizes is enabled, 5 more text sizes become available."
Verifier evidence (high): The quote itself ("7 available text sizes... If larger accessibility sizes is enabled, 5 more become available") directly supports the claim's arithmetic (7+5=12). WebSearch corroboration from independent technical sources (createwithswift.com, useyourloaf.com) confirms the same breakdown: standard sizes xSmall/Small/Medium/Large/xLarge/xxLarge/xxxLarge (7) plus accessibility sizes AX1-AX5 (5), matching Apple's UIContentSizeCategory enum which has exactly 12 cases. No contradicting evidence found in search. Source is Apple's own WWDC24 session "Get started with Dynamic Type" (developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10074/), an appropriate primary source for this factual/technical claim, and the WWDC24 session date confirms this is current (not superseded by any later Dynamic Type ramp change). Not a marketing claim — purely a technical enumeration fact.

### [7] Apple's stated guidance is that horizontal layouts should dynamically switch to a vertical stack at accessibility text sizes so each element can take the full display width — a layout decision, not a font-size decision.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10074/ (primary)
Quote: "When the text size increases, the layout dynamically switches to a vertical stack allowing each cell to take the entire width of the display."
Verifier evidence (high): Direct WebFetch of the primary source (developer.apple.com/videos/play/wwdc2024/10074/, 'Get started with Dynamic Type', WWDC 2024) returns the exact quoted sentence verbatim: 'When the text size increases, the layout dynamically switches to a vertical stack allowing each cell to take the entire width of the display.' The same fetch surfaces a second, independent corroborating example from the same session (the 'Figure' cells demo) with an accompanying SwiftUI code sample: dynamicTypeSize.isAccessibilitySize ? AnyLayout(VStackLayout(...)) : AnyLayout(HStackLayout(...)), explicitly switching HStack→VStack at accessibility sizes 'to provide more width to the text ... while avoiding truncations.' This is a 'Get started with...' tutorial/guidance session aimed at teaching developers/designers the recommended technique, not an isolated anecdote — two worked examples plus a reusable code pattern support characterizing it as Apple's stated guidance, and the claim's framing ('layout decision, not a font-size decision') accurately reflects that the fix is switching stack axis, not just scaling text. Source is a primary Apple developer resource, content is current (WWDC 2024, no superseding guidance found), and is technical/tutorial content, not marketing.

### [8] Apple states that iOS Dynamic Type reaches sizes larger than 200% of the default at the AX3 accessibility size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at AX5 — giving designers concrete numeric targets for the top of the Dynamic Type ramp.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/ (primary)
Quote: "Many accessibility guidelines recommend allowing users to enlarge text to 200% or larger than the default size. Dynamic Type on iOS, for example, reaches sizes larger than 200% at the AX3 size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at the AX5 size."
Verifier evidence (high): WebFetch of the cited primary source (developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/) confirms the quote verbatim: "Dynamic Type on iOS, for example, reaches sizes larger than 200% at the AX3 size, and allows body text sizes over 300% at the AX5 size." This is Apple's own official App Store Connect help documentation (a primary source), and the claim is a faithful paraphrase with no numeric distortion — it doesn't overstate or misread the quote. Cross-check against known Dynamic Type point sizes corroborates the math (default body ~17pt; AX3 body ~40pt ≈ 235%; AX5 body ~53pt ≈ 311%), and third-party sources (uxdesign.cc, createwithswift.com, useyourloaf.com) independently confirm AX3/AX5 involve dramatic, layout-breaking scale increases consistent with these percentages. No contradicting evidence found. The claim's closing clause ("giving designers concrete numeric targets...") is a reasonable interpretive gloss, not a factual overreach, since these are indeed the only percentage figures Apple publishes for the top of the ramp.

### [9] Apple's stated layout guidance for large accessibility text sizes is that side-by-side elements should reflow — wrapping onto a new line or being laid out vertically instead of horizontally — because they overlap when enlarged.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/ (primary)
Quote: "Smaller side-by-side elements may overlap when enlarged, so consider wrapping them onto a new line or laying them out vertically rather than horizontally."
Verifier evidence (high): Direct WebFetch of the cited primary source (developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/) confirms the exact quote verbatim: "Smaller side-by-side elements may overlap when enlarged, so consider wrapping them onto a new line or laying them out vertically rather than horizontally. In the example below, the layout of the message sender, receiver, and date changes from horizontal to vertical to support larger text sizes." This is Apple's own official App Store Connect accessibility evaluation criteria documentation (part of Apple's "Larger Text" accessibility evaluation criteria section on responsive design principles), not a secondary/marketing source. The claim statement is a faithful, non-overreaching paraphrase of the quote — it doesn't add unsupported specifics (e.g., no exact size thresholds claimed beyond what's quoted). A follow-up WebSearch corroborated the page's existence and topic (Larger Text accessibility evaluation criteria, Dynamic Type up to 300%+, testing at accessibility sizes) with no contradicting guidance found from Apple or elsewhere. Source quality (Apple's own developer documentation) is appropriate for this claim's strength, which is a modest, verifiable documentation-quote claim, not an extraordinary one.

### [10] Apple's criteria treat truncation as a failure condition at large text sizes: text must not truncate to the point of being unreadable or ambiguous, and the recommended remedy is wrapping to two or more lines.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/ (primary)
Quote: "Avoid truncating text to the point that it becomes unreadable or ambiguous for the user. Consider allowing the text to wrap to two or more lines instead of truncation."
Verifier evidence (high): Fetched the primary source directly (developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect/manage-app-accessibility/larger-text-evaluation-criteria/). Confirmed the page contains a section titled "Avoid overlapping text and excessive or unusable truncation" with the exact quoted text: "Avoid truncating text to the point that it becomes unreadable or ambiguous for the user. Consider allowing the text to wrap to two or more lines instead of truncation." This sits within Apple's Larger Text evaluation criteria used for the App Store's accessibility nutrition labels, confirming it as a real evaluation criterion (not marketing copy) that developers/designers are assessed against. A supplementary WebSearch corroborated the page's existence and content (App Store Connect Help, part of the Larger Text/Dynamic Type nutrition-label criteria referencing testing at largest Dynamic Type sizes and truncation/overlap failures). The claim's wording ("failure condition," "recommended remedy is wrapping to two or more lines") is a faithful, non-overreaching paraphrase of the quoted text — it does not add unsupported specifics (e.g., it doesn't claim truncation is always disqualifying; the fetched page notes truncation is acceptable if full text is accessible elsewhere, which the claim doesn't contradict). Source is primary (Apple developer documentation), directly on-topic, and current (this Accessibility Nutrition Labels evaluation-criteria series is Apple's active, current guidance as of 2025-2026, not a superseded page).

### [11] Apple explicitly disallows relying on system-provided magnification (Zoom, Hover Text) to satisfy the Larger Text requirement — the app's own layout must scale, which is a native-specific requirement with no direct web-checklist equivalent (browser zoom/reflow is normally an acceptable web mechanism under WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10).

Verified evidence answers only HALF ONE of the two-part question (native platform accessibility as a design decision) in depth; HALF TWO (EAA, ADA Title II, Section 508, WCAG 2.2 legal status) has zero surviving claims — not even a refuted one — so it is effectively unresearched in this evidence set. On HALF ONE: Apple's Dynamic Type ramp is fully specified (7 standard sizes + 5 accessibility sizes AX1–AX5; Body text 17pt→53pt, ~311% at AX5, crossing 200% already at AX3), and Apple's HIG/App Store Connect docs give designers concrete, quoted instructions to switch side-by-side layouts to vertical stacks, allow text to wrap to 2+ lines instead of truncating, and never rely on system Zoom/Hover Text to claim "Larger Text" support — a native-specific rule with no web equivalent, since browser zoom/reflow is an accepted mechanism for WCAG 1.4.4/1.4.10. VoiceOver guidance requires two separate designer decisions not implied by any web checklist: explicit grouping/ordering of elements (default order is layout-derived, top-to-bottom/left-to-right, so unpaired image+caption elements read as two disjoint streams), and keeping accessibility labels free of control-type/state words (which belong in traits, not labels, to avoid doubled speech like "checkbox, checkbox") while treating value as a separate channel from label. Android 14 raised max font scaling to 200% via a nonlinear curve that breaks sp-value additivity (4sp+20sp≠24sp) and requires apps to be explicitly re-tested at 200%, and Android's own design guidance sets a 48dp minimum touch target (extending past the visual bounds if needed) and a 12sp body-text floor — a stricter, more literally enforced regime than Apple's 44×44pt/28×28pt table, which Apple itself frames as aspirational ("strive to meet") rather than a hard minimum.</summary>

findings.claim: VoiceOver's default reading order is derived from layout (top-to-bottom, left-to-right in the user's active locale), so a designer must explicitly decide grouping - auditing the UI for relationships conveyed only by visual proximity/alignment and describing those relationships to VoiceOver - or visually-paired elements (e.g. image plus caption) will be read as two separate streams (all images, then all captions).
findings.evidence: Two related claims from the same live HIG VoiceOver page, both verified 3-0 with verbatim quote matches (including reproducing Apple's own 'in the their' typo, confirming direct transcription). Squarely a designer-level decision distinct from developer implementation: Apple frames it as 'Specify how elements are grouped, ordered, or linked' at the design-guideline level and defers the how (accessibilityElements, sortPriority APIs) to separate developer-guidance links.

findings.claim: Apple's VoiceOver evaluation criteria require a label distinct from a control's value (label names the field, e.g. phone number; value carries content, e.g. 555-555-1212), and separately prohibit encoding control type or state (e.g. checkbox, checked) inside the label - that information belongs in accessibility traits - because duplicating it in the label produces redundant doubled speech like checkbox-checkbox.
findings.evidence: Both claims verified 3-0 with verbatim quotes from Apple's App Store Connect VoiceOver evaluation criteria page, independently corroborated by third-party iOS-accessibility practitioner sources (Deque, mobilea11y, 24a11y). Directly answers the requested label-vs-hint-vs-value distinction, though the source is Apple's App Store Connect help center rather than the HIG page itself - still primary and current, a different Apple property.

findings.claim: Android 14 raised maximum font scaling to 200 percent and applies a nonlinear scaling curve so large text scales less aggressively than small text (preserving type hierarchy and preventing cutoff/unreadable oversized text); a direct consequence is that sp values are no longer additive (4sp+20sp may not equal 24sp), so sp must not be used for padding or view heights that assume implicit padding, and apps must still be explicitly UI-tested at the 200 percent maximum even if they already use sp (which gets the improvement automatically).
findings.evidence: Three tightly related claims, all verified 3-0 with verbatim quote matches from the same live Android 14 features page. Surfaces a native-only pitfall - non-additive sp arithmetic breaking padding/height math - that has no web-CSS analogue and that a web-derived accessibility checklist would not catch.

findings.claim: Android's official design guidance sets a minimum touch target of 48dp and explicitly requires it be met even when it extends past the visible bounds of the UI element; separately, font sizes should be declared in sp (not dp/px) so the user's OS font-scaling setting applies at all, with a floor of 12sp for body text aligned to the Material type scale.
findings.evidence: The 48dp claim verified 3-0 verbatim; the sp/12sp claim verified 2-1 (verbatim quote confirmed, dissent likely on 'requires' vs the source's softer 'specify' framing). Requested WCAG-comparison point: Android's 48dp is commonly compared to WCAG 2.5.5/2.5.8 target-size criteria, but no primary source in this pass directly bridges Android's 48dp to a specific WCAG success-criterion number - that mapping is common practice, not confirmed here against WCAG text itself.

findings.claim: No verified evidence exists on HALF TWO of the research question: the European Accessibility Act's June 2025 applicability date and scope, the microenterprise exemption, EN 301 549's relationship to WCAG, the DOJ ADA Title II web rule (28 CFR 35 subpart H), its named technical standard and size-tiered compliance deadlines, Section 508's current referenced standard, or whether any binding instrument names WCAG 2.2.
findings.evidence: Zero claims about EAA/EUR-Lex, ada.gov/Federal Register, or ETSI EN 301 549 appear in either the confirmed or refuted claim lists supplied for synthesis - a gap in the underlying research, not a disagreement resolved against those claims. All 19 confirmed and 6 refuted claims cluster exclusively on Apple/Android native accessibility topics (HALF ONE). This half of the question is unanswered and needs a dedicated research pass against EUR-Lex, ada.gov, and ETSI primary texts before it can be reported with any confidence.

input.caveats: Two HALF ONE items landed at split 2-1 votes rather than unanimous 3-0 (the WWDC24 vertical-stack claim, and the Android sp/12sp floor claim) - treat those two as slightly less certain, though in both cases the dissent appears to be about wording strength ('requires' vs Apple/Google's softer 'consider'/'specify'), not about the underlying fact. Several claims require careful verb-softening when reused: Apple's 44x44pt minimum is aspirational (strive to meet), not a hard floor; the 200/140 percent text-enlargement target is Ideally, not must; and the 28x28pt visionOS control-size figure conflicts with a 60x60pt hit-region figure on Apple's own Buttons page, so control size and tappable hit region must not be conflated when comparing to Android's 48dp. Six other candidate claims (VoiceOver rotor/heading structure, reachability of every element via rotor plus linear navigation, custom-actions-vs-individual-navigation for grouped elements, Android decorative-image null-description convention, Android semantic heading markup for structural navigation) were tested and refuted (0-3 or 1-2 votes) - the specific wording researched did not hold up, not necessarily that the underlying practice is false; these topics remain open for re-research with more precise claims. Most significant caveat: HALF TWO of the research question (EAA, ADA Title II, Section 508, WCAG 2.2 binding status) has no surviving evidence at all in this claim set - the findings above cover HALF ONE only. Time-sensitivity: the Apple HIG and App Store Connect sources show live edit dates as recent as December 2025 and are current as of the August 2026 fetch; the Android 14 features page describes a 2023-era platform change that remains current stable guidance through 2026 with no indication of reversal.
